glossary.meaning: The overseer: the one who watches over a community's table and its unity. Whether every church should have one such man, or the elders should share that trust, was still being argued.
The elders who share the governing of a community. In some churches they were a council holding the whole trust. In others they gathered around one overseer.
The thanksgiving: the meal of bread and cup over which thanks is given. The community returns to this table again and again, to be formed once more into one body.
Before the water came the teaching of the two ways: a way of life and a way of death, with a great difference between them.
The Latin word a Roman governor used for two enslaved women he had tortured. They were Christians in some known service. No one wrote down what the women called themselves.
glossary.world_word: ministrae (Pliny's word, not the community's own)

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia, to the emperor Trajan
pull_quotes.text: So I thought it all the more needed to question two female slaves. They were called deaconesses, ministrae. I did this even with torture, to find out the truth. But I found nothing but a depraved superstition that went too far. So I have put off further inquiry, and I have turned to you for advice.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: the manual known as the Didache, or the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles
pull_quotes.text: There are two ways: one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. The way of life is this. First, you shall love God, who made you; second, your neighbor as yourself. And all the things you would not want to happen to you, you also must not do to another.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: the manual known as the Didache
pull_quotes.text: Now, about the Thanksgiving - the Eucharist - give thanks this way. First, over the cup: We thank you, our Father, for the holy vine of David your servant, which you made known to us through Jesus your Servant. To you be the glory forever.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, writing to Victor of Rome
pull_quotes.text: As for us, we keep the exact day with great care, adding nothing and taking nothing away. For in Asia great luminaries have gone to their rest, and they will rise again on the day the Lord comes. And I too, Polycrates, the least of you all, follow the tradition of my relatives, some of whom I have succeeded. Seven of my relatives were bishops, and I am the eighth. My relatives always kept the day when the people put away the leaven. I myself, brothers, am sixty-five years old in the Lord. I have met the brothers in every part of the world, and I have read through all of Holy Scripture. So I am not frightened by the things people say to terrify us. For those greater than I have said: "We ought to obey God rather than men."

cite.text: One of us, Ignatius, put it with great force. Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pilate, truly crucified, and truly died. Some among our neighbors said he only seemed to suffer. Ignatius answered that he was truly raised, and that the same Father will raise us in the same way. Others among us said the same thing more quietly. When we gave thanks over the cup, the eucharistia, we thanked the Father for the holy vine of David, his servant, which he made known to us through Jesus, his servant.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Who was Jesus, to you and your people?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: He was a real man, not an idea. Ignatius wrote against people who said Jesus only seemed to be a man, and he put it as hard as it can be put. Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pilate, truly crucified, and truly died. And Ignatius said he was truly raised, the same way we ourselves will be raised, by the same Father. When we gave thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we thanked the Father for the holy vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus.

cite.text: Ignatius called Jesus Christ our God again and again, in how he opened his letters and in how he closed them. It was not one passing phrase; he reached for it often. But it was worship, not an argument worked out. No one whose writing survives explained how calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God, with there being one God. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had worked out how he could be God when the Father is God, and God is one.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Was Jesus God? Did you believe in the Trinity?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Ignatius called Jesus Christ our God again and again. He did it when he opened his letters and when he closed them. It was a phrase of worship. That word of yours, Trinity, is not one we used. How calling Jesus God fits with calling the Father God, none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We did call him God. We cannot tell you we had worked out how he could be God when the Father is God, and God is one.

cite.text: We cannot promise you a moment of sudden certainty. For the one among us who wrote about it, belief came at the end of a long search. Justin said he had already gone looking through other philosophies. Then an old man spoke with him, and, in his own phrase, a flame was kindled in his soul. As he turned the old man's words over in his mind, he found this to be the one safe and worthwhile path. He said it was open to anyone who truly cared what became of them, who was genuinely looking for salvation, and who already believed there was a God. We should say plainly, though: this is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: I want to believe in Jesus, but I can't. What would you say to me?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We cannot promise you a moment of sudden certainty. Justin, the one among us who wrote about his own path, says he went looking through other philosophies first. Then an old man spoke with him, and, in his own phrase, a flame was kindled in his soul. He turned the old man's words over in his mind and found this the one safe and worthwhile way. He told the man he was speaking with that anyone who cares what becomes of them, who is eagerly looking for salvation, and who believes in God may come to know the Christ of God. His is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had.

quiet.statement: Enslaved people were among us. Our instruction spoke to them directly, in the same breath as everyone else. Two enslaved women among us were called ministrae - servants, deacons - and when a Roman governor wanted to know what we did, it was those two he had tortured for answers. So we can tell you they were here. We can tell you they served, and that they were tortured. What we cannot give you is a single word any of them chose to write or say for themselves. What an enslaved sister or brother made of our teaching, or of our meal - none of that survives in their own voice. Everything we know of them passed through other hands. We would rather tell you that plainly than put words in their mouths now.

who_speaks.text: Four figures anchor this world's own voice. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, argued hard for one-bishop unity while under guard toward his own execution. Hermas, a freedman in Rome, wrote down visions about doubt, mercy, and one further chance to repent. Justin was a philosopher who kept his philosopher's cloak. He described a Sunday gathering to the emperor himself, and died for what he defended. Polycarp led the church at Smyrna. He refused to curse Christ before a hostile crowd. He is remembered alongside a very different man, one his own community would not hold up as an example.

documented_stories.teaser: Rome burns in a great fire. The Roman historian Tacitus reports that Nero blamed a group the crowd called Christians, and had them put to death with cruelty.
documented_stories.tellable_as: After the Great Fire of Rome, Nero blamed a group the crowd called Christians. He had them put to death with cruelty meant as a show.
documented_stories.telling:
In 64 a great fire burned through Rome. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing some fifty years later, says a rumor spread that the fire had been set on orders. To get rid of that rumor, Nero shifted the blame onto a group the crowd called Christians.

Tacitus wrote from outside our communities, and he had his own reasons for portraying Nero as monstrous. What he describes is one episode under one emperor. We cannot be sure that Christians, as a group known by that name, were punished after the fire. A more general memory from later years may have been attached to it.

Tacitus describes the Christians as hated for their vile acts. Those who confessed were arrested first, he reports, and on their information a great number were convicted. In his reading, they were condemned less for arson than for hatred of humankind.

No source names a single Christian who died in these events. Tacitus says they were put to death with cruelty meant as a show. Some were wrapped in the skins of beasts and torn apart by dogs. Others were fastened to crosses, or set alight as torches after dark.
documented_stories.title: Nero Blames the Christians for the Fire
documented_stories.when: 64 (Tacitus wrote about fifty years later; we cannot be sure a separate persecution tied to the fire took place in 64)

documented_stories.teaser: This scene is pieced together from the Didache. A community following its order gives thanks over the cup first, then the bread. No story of a supper appears in its prayers.
documented_stories.tellable_as: In a community that followed the Didache's order, thanks was given first over the cup, then over the bread. No story of a supper or a betrayal appears in the prayers. They speak of the vine, of life and knowledge, and of a scattered people gathered into one.
documented_stories.telling:
A community that followed the Didache gave thanks over the cup first. "We thank you, our Father, for the holy vine of David your servant," the prayer begins. This picture is pieced together from the Didache's own instructions.

Then came thanks over the broken bread, for the life and knowledge made known through Jesus. The prayer says this broken bread was once scattered over the hills, and was gathered together to become one. In the same way, the prayer asks God to gather the Church from the ends of the earth into his kingdom. Nowhere in these prayers does anyone tell the story of a supper or a betrayal.

Only the baptized ate or drank of this thanksgiving. After all had eaten their fill, a longer thanksgiving followed, for God's holy name and for knowledge and faith and immortality. It closed with the community's own cry, Maran atha, and then Amen.

Every Lord's day the community gathered to break bread and give thanks, after first confessing their sins. Anyone at odds with another had to be reconciled before joining in.
documented_stories.title: Thanks Over the Cup Before the Bread
documented_stories.when: c. 80-120 (the usual dating of the Didache; we cannot fix it closer than 50 to 150)

documented_stories.teaser: Hegesippus, writing long afterward, tells how Domitian hears that kin of Jesus, of David's line, are alive. Two grandsons of Judas, called the brother of Jesus, show him rough farmers' hands, and he lets them go.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the day the emperor sent for Jesus' family and found two farmers with calloused hands
documented_stories.telling:
This story comes from Hegesippus, a Christian of Palestine who wrote it down perhaps eighty years after it happened. It survives only because the bishop Eusebius quoted him long afterward.

Some of Jesus' own family were still alive. They were grandsons of Judas, who was called his brother. They were reported to the emperor Domitian as being of the line of David. That mattered to Domitian, because he dreaded the coming of Christ as Herod had, so they were brought before him and questioned.

Were they of David's family? They said they were. Asked what they owned, they said they had only nine thousand denarii between them, and not in coin. That was the value of a piece of land of only thirty-nine acres. They still paid the dues on it, and they lived by working it themselves.

Then they held out their hands to show him the rough skin and the corns raised by constant labor. He asked them about Christ's kingdom and when it would come. They told him it was not of this world or of the earth, but belonged to heaven and the angels. It would appear at the end of time.

Domitian passed no sentence. He treated them with contempt, as beneath his notice, and he let them go and called off the persecution. Once they were released, they became leaders of the churches.
documented_stories.title: Two Farmers Before the Emperor

documented_stories.teaser: The church at Rome writes at length to Corinth, which has removed several elders from office. It argues that men who served blamelessly should not have been removed.
documented_stories.tellable_as: The church at Rome writes a long letter to the church at Corinth. Corinth had removed several of its own elders from office. Rome argues that men who served blamelessly should not have been removed.
documented_stories.telling:
The church at Corinth had removed some of its presbyters, its elders, from office. The church at Rome answered with a long letter. It names no author, though later tradition says Clement wrote it. We usually date it around 96, though it may be as late as 140.

Rome's letter says the presbyters had served blamelessly and with honor. Only Rome's letter survives, and Corinth's own side of the dispute is lost.

The letter takes up the removal directly. It gives example after example of jealousy and strife destroying what unity had built. Rome wrote as one church to another, out of concern. It could only appeal, and it gave no orders the way a later church authority would.

Corinth's action, the letter argues, broke proper order, and it calls on those who started the revolt to submit to the presbyters.
documented_stories.title: Rome Writes to Corinth About Removed Elders
documented_stories.when: c. 96 (the traditional dating; we cannot fix it closer than before 70 to 140)

documented_stories.teaser: Letters under Ignatius's name say that he, a bishop of Antioch, was marched under armed guard toward Rome. He writes ahead to urge the church there not to try to save him.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A condemned bishop is marched under guard toward death in Rome. On the way he writes seven letters. He urges unity around one bishop, and he sees his death as the finishing of his formation.
documented_stories.telling:
In the letters that carry his name, Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, says that he was condemned. He was sent under armed guard on the long road to Rome. There he expected to be thrown to the beasts in the arena. We cannot be sure he wrote them himself. They may have been written later, in Rome, under his name.

He says he was bound to ten leopards, by which he means his band of soldiers. They only grew worse, he says, when they were treated kindly. Churches came out to meet him along the way, and at Smyrna he was met by delegations from Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles.

On the road he wrote at least seven letters that survive. He urged each community to gather around one bishop and one eucharist. He pressed the point hard because that unity was still being argued over. He believed his coming death gave his words unusual weight.

He asked Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, to write for him to the nearby churches. He thanked the church at Smyrna for welcoming his companions and for not being ashamed of his chains. He sent a letter ahead to the church at Rome, asking them not to step in to save his life. He called himself the wheat of God. He asked to be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, so that he might be found the pure bread of Christ.
documented_stories.title: A Condemned Bishop Asks Rome Not to Save Him
documented_stories.when: c. 107-117 (traditional dating; we cannot be sure who wrote the letters or when)

documented_stories.teaser: Polycarp writes to the church at Philippi. He is sending them the letters of Ignatius that his church has collected, as they had asked.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Polycarp of Smyrna sent the church at Philippi the letters of Ignatius that his own church had collected. The Philippians had asked for them.
documented_stories.telling:
The Philippians asked for the letters of Ignatius, which the community at Smyrna had collected. Polycarp of Smyrna answered their request in a letter of his own to the church at Philippi.

We cannot be sure of the letter's date. It may be two letters joined into one. Polycarp opens it in his own name and that of the presbyters who are with him. He never calls himself bishop, though Ignatius writes to him as one, and Smyrna's letter on his death calls him its bishop.

He writes that he has sent the letters Ignatius wrote to Smyrna, along with all the others they had, just as the Philippians asked. The letters went with his own, and he told the Philippians they could gain a great deal from them.
documented_stories.title: Polycarp Sends Ignatius's Letters to Philippi
documented_stories.when: c. 107-140 (the letter's date is uncertain, and it may be two letters joined)

documented_stories.teaser: Pliny, a Roman governor, is not sure how to treat Christians brought before him. He has two enslaved women tortured to learn what the community did. Then he writes to the emperor Trajan for advice.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A Roman governor is unsure what to do about Christians brought before him. He has two enslaved women tortured to learn what the community did. Then he writes to the emperor.
documented_stories.telling:
Pliny the Younger was the Roman governor of Bithynia and Pontus. Writing to the emperor Trajan, he says he was unsure how to handle accusations against Christians, so he asked the emperor. He had already questioned those accused, and executed those who held to the name after repeated warnings.

Some of the accused told him they had once been Christians but had given it up. They said they used to meet on a fixed day before dawn and sing a song in turns to Christ as God. They had bound themselves by an oath to commit no theft, robbery or adultery, and never to break faith or refuse to return a deposit. Then they parted, and later met again to share a meal of ordinary food, which they said was harmless. What that meal was, we cannot say for certain.

To learn the truth, he tortured two enslaved women who were called ministrae. It may be a title, deaconesses, though that reading is disputed. The women left no words of their own, and we have only what Pliny chose to record. What he found, in his own words, was "nothing but a depraved superstition that went too far."

Trajan's reply survives, and it says Pliny had acted rightly. Christians were not to be hunted out. Those accused and convicted were to be punished, and anyone who denied the name and proved it by act was to be pardoned. Anonymous accusations were to be refused as a very bad precedent.
documented_stories.title: A Governor Writes to the Emperor About Christians

documented_stories.teaser: Justin tells the emperor what happens when his community gathers on the day named for the sun. They hear readings and a talk, pray, give thanks over bread and wine, and make a collection for the needy.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Justin tells the emperor and the Senate what happens when his community gathers on the day named for the sun. There is reading, a sermon, common prayer, thanksgiving over bread and wine, and a collection for those in need.
documented_stories.telling:
Justin wrote to the emperor and the Roman Senate to defend Christian practice. He tells them plainly what his community at Rome does on the day named for the sun. He does not say whether the churches of Antioch or Asia Minor followed the same order.

On that day, those who live in the cities and in the countryside gather in one place. The memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read for as long as time permits. Then the one presiding gives a talk, urging the people to imitate these good things, and all rise together and pray.

Bread and wine and water are brought. The one presiding offers prayers and thanksgivings according to his ability, and the people give their assent by saying Amen. Those who have means and are willing give what they choose, and the gifts are left with him.

The one presiding cares for orphans and widows, the sick, those in prison and strangers passing through. In a word, Justin writes, he looks after everyone who is in need.
documented_stories.title: A Sunday Gathering as Justin Describes It

documented_stories.teaser: The letter from Smyrna that honors Polycarp also names Quintus. He came forward for trial and lost his nerve at the sight of the beasts. The letter says the gospel does not teach people to give themselves up.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Before the letter praises Polycarp's own courage, it names a different man first. He came forward for trial on his own. Then he lost his nerve, when he actually saw the beasts.
documented_stories.telling:
Before Polycarp's own flight and arrest, the letter from Smyrna that honors his death tells of another man.

Quintus was a Phrygian who had lately come from Phrygia. He forced himself and some others to come forward for trial of their own accord. When he actually saw the wild beasts, he lost his nerve. After much urging, the proconsul persuaded him to swear the oath and offer sacrifice.

The letter says plainly that the church does not praise those who give themselves up, because the Gospel does not teach people to do so. Polycarp did the opposite. When he first heard that he was being sought, he was not troubled at all. He meant to stay in the city, but at the wish of many he agreed to leave.

He went to a country house not far from the city. There he stayed with a few companions, praying night and day. When his pursuers came near, he moved to another house. He did not go looking for arrest. He was found only after two young men of his household were seized, and one of them, under torture, told his pursuers where he was.
documented_stories.title: The Man Who Volunteered and Broke

documented_stories.teaser: The church at Smyrna tells how Polycarp, its aged leader, refused to curse Christ and was put to death. The account says the fire arched around him. The community kept his bones.
documented_stories.tellable_as: The church at Smyrna remembers its aged bishop Polycarp refusing to curse Christ before the crowd. He was burned, then finished with a dagger. Afterward the church hoped to gather each year at the place where his bones were laid.
documented_stories.telling:
This is how the church at Smyrna remembered Polycarp, its aged bishop, in a letter to the church at Philomelium. It is told in the style our tradition used to honor its martyrs, and no outside account survives to check it.

His community urged Polycarp to hide, and he withdrew for a time, until someone in his own household gave him away under torture. Before the proconsul he was pressed to swear by Caesar's fortune, curse Christ and be spared. Polycarp answered that he had served Christ for eighty-six years, and Christ had never done him any wrong. How then, he asked, could he blaspheme his King and his Savior?

The crowd first cried out for a lion, but the official in charge said it was not lawful, because the wild-beast shows were already over. So they cried out that he should be burned alive. When the fire was lit, the account says it formed an arch around him, like the sail of a ship filled by the wind. An executioner was sent to finish him with a dagger, and the account says so much blood came out that it put out the fire.

Afterward the community gathered his bones, which they held more precious than the finest jewels, and laid them in a fitting place. There they hoped to gather each year, as they were able, to keep the day of his martyrdom. They would remember those who had finished the course and prepare those still to walk it.
documented_stories.title: Polycarp Refuses to Curse Christ

floor_note.text: This world affirmed a real man, really killed, and really raised. Against a rival teaching that said Christ's body only seemed real, one of its own bishops answered as hard as it could be answered: truly born, truly crucified, truly raised. And in worship, the same bishop called Jesus Christ "our God," again and again, in how he opened his letters and how he closed them. But none of this world's own surviving voices ever worked out how calling Jesus God fit together with calling the Father God. No council had yet met to decide a question like that. What can be said plainly is what they confessed. What cannot be said is that they had settled how.

A short teaching manual, likely from one community. One copy of 1056 keeps almost all of it. Scholars date it between about 50 and 150.
Bishop of Antioch. Seven letters in his name say he was marched under guard toward death in Rome. Their author and date are disputed.
A church leader at Smyrna. His own letter to the Philippians survives, and his church told how he was put to death.
A philosopher who kept wearing his gown as a Christian. He described a Sunday gathering in a letter to the emperor. He died about 165.
A Roman historian who despised Christians. Around 116, he wrote about the Great Fire of 64.
Roman emperor at the Great Fire of Rome in 64. Tacitus says rumor blamed him, and he turned the blame on Christians.
A Roman governor, not a Christian. He wrote to the emperor about Christians around 111 to 113.
The Roman emperor who received Pliny's letter and answered it.
A modern scholar of the early church at Rome. He reads it as many small household groups that only slowly came under one bishop.

The Roman emperor in this account. Hegesippus says he dreaded the coming of Christ, and that this is why he had the two men questioned.

A writer of the second century. We know his work because a later bishop, Eusebius, quoted it.

legacy.text: This world's own authority question did not stay open forever. By around 200 CE, one bishop had become the common pattern almost everywhere, including in Rome. Rome had once been led by a council of elders, with nothing felt to be missing. No text says how or when that change was actually felt. Only the older, argued option's own quiet disappearance is visible.

This world's own texts did not survive evenly. Ignatius's letters mattered so much to the later, settled office he argued for that it took a two-century scholarly fight just to prove they were genuine. First Clement was copied into a great Bible manuscript. The Shepherd of Hermas was once read as scripture by three major later teachers. Later, it was moved instead to the shelf newcomers were given to read - a real demotion, though not the outright ban later memory sometimes assumes. The Didache, this world's own teaching manual, disappeared from use for roughly eighteen centuries. What survived best was not always what mattered most at the time. It was what a later settlement found useful to keep.

read_first.note: This world's sharpest surviving voice, and its most contested - a corpus urgently arguing for one-bishop unity, under a genuine three-way scholarly dispute over who wrote it and when.

source.citation: Ignatius of Antioch, the seven letters (shorter recension), Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), Roberts-Donaldson series

read_first.note: Rome's own long letter correcting a sister church, in a plural elders' own voice - this world's earliest surviving Christian writing outside the New Testament, and its clearest picture of a council-governed community.

source.citation: First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, trans. Roberts-Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885); the portion recovered from Codex Hierosolymitanus, rev. John Keith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 9 (1896)

read_first.note: The one outside account of this world's worship, and its harshest evidence: what a Roman governor learned about a Sunday gathering by torturing two enslaved women, and the emperor's own reply telling him not to go looking for more.

source.citation: Pliny the Younger, Letters 10.96-10.97, with Trajan's rescript, as printed in A. C. McGiffert's note to Eusebius, Church History III.33, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 1 (1890)

relations_summary.text: This world's own record closes just as a different Christian world takes shape in Alexandria. That world formed people through one teacher's close relationship with a student, not through letters and household worship. This world's own texts never mention it at all. One figure here, Justin, also belongs to a second, not-yet-built tradition: philosophers who argued directly with Roman emperors. This world uses only what his writing happens to say about worship and about rival teachers. It does not use his fuller philosophical argument.

sourcing.text: This world's record is moderate to rich on communal life - letters, church order, worship practice - but its most vivid material leans on one contested corpus: Ignatius's seven letters, whose authorship and dating remain a genuine, three-way dispute among scholars. Individual, first-person voice stays thin throughout. No woman speaks in her own words. No enslaved member does either - two enslaved women are named only by their torturer's own word for their office. No non-literate believer, who made up most of this movement, speaks for themselves at all. What survives is a city record, written by the literate few.

story.text: From about 70 to 200 CE, Christians gathered in households. They lived in Antioch and Syria, in the cities of western Asia Minor, and in Rome. Letters and travelers kept them joined as one. The last of the apostles' generation was passing, and no central body ruled these churches.

These churches held that legitimate teaching and practice must trace back to what the apostles had testified. Rome's letter to Corinth sets out a chain. God sent Christ, Christ sent the apostles, and the apostles appointed successors. Ignatius, a bishop of Antioch, writes to several churches. He tells them to be subject to the bishop, as the apostles were subject to Christ.

The surviving letters give two different answers to who should lead once the apostles were gone. Ignatius's letters put one bishop at the center, with elders and deacons beside him. One letter says the elders fit the bishop as strings fit a harp. In Rome, the surviving letters show a council of elders leading together. Ignatius addresses Polycarp, a church leader at Smyrna, as a bishop. Polycarp's own letter names him only beside the elders with him.

Letters held these scattered households together. The church at Rome wrote at length to Corinth, which had removed some of its elders from office. Rome argued that men who had served blamelessly should not have been removed. Seven surviving letters under Ignatius's name say he wrote them on a guarded journey toward Rome. Later, Polycarp sent the Philippians the letters of Ignatius that his church held, because they had asked for them.

Giving thanks over bread and cup stood at the center of these gatherings, and its order changed from one household to the next. One community's manual, the Didache, gives thanks over the cup before the bread. It tells no story of a supper or a betrayal. Ignatius says that only a thanksgiving the bishop leads, or entrusts to another, counts as proper. Justin, a philosopher in Rome, describes a fuller Sunday gathering there.

The danger from the state was always there, but the actual incidents came and went. Tacitus, a Roman historian, reports that Nero blamed the Great Fire of Rome in 64 on a group the crowd called Christians. A great number, he says, were convicted and put to death. No source names one of them. About fifty years later, Pliny, the governor of Bithynia and Pontus, wrote to the emperor Trajan for guidance. He found, in his words, "nothing but a depraved superstition that went too far." Trajan replied that Christians were not to be sought out, though those accused and convicted were to be punished.

Some communities read a death for the name as the completion of a life. Ignatius writes that he wants to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that he may be found the pure bread of Christ. The church at Smyrna told how Polycarp died. Its letter says the community kept his bones in a fitting place. They hoped to gather there each year, as they were able, to keep the day of his death. The same letter names Quintus, who came forward for trial and lost his nerve at the sight of the beasts. It says the gospel does not teach people to give themselves up. Only these two inside accounts survive, Ignatius's letters and Smyrna's letter, and both come from Antioch and Asia Minor.

By about 200, one bishop was becoming the dominant pattern, even in Rome. One modern scholar, Peter Lampe, thinks Rome may not have had a single bishop before Victor, its bishop from 189 to 199. The texts of these churches do not say how or when Rome changed. From about 180, writers in other regions argued from an apostolic line they treated as already secure.

dates.display: the letters are traditionally dated c. 107-117; one scholarly camp redates them to the 130s-140s, another holds them pseudepigraphic compositions of c. 160-180
dates.note: deliberately no single year: the three positions are not a range, and collapsing them would settle in a data field the dispute every telling must carry. These bound the LETTERS, not the man's life.

names.name: Ignatius of Antioch (the middle-recension letters; authenticity and dating three-way split)

voices.hedge: Did Ignatius write when he says he did? Scholars disagree. Some hold the traditional date. Some place it decades later. Some think the whole set of letters was invented long after his own time. Every claim about him carries that open dispute forward.
voices.text: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch. He was taken under armed guard toward execution in Rome. Along the way, he wrote seven letters that survive. He urged every community he addressed to gather around one bishop, one altar, one eucharist. He read his own coming death as the completion of a life already given over, not as something to fear.

dates.display: the Shepherd was composed c. 90-150, possibly in stages
dates.note: these bound the WORK, not the man - his own dates are not attested

voices.hedge: The Shepherd was written in stages, across roughly sixty years, not all at once. So 'Hermas' may be closer to a small tradition than to one man's single testimony. His own life dates are not known at all. Only the work's own writing window is.
voices.text: Hermas was a freedman in Rome. He wrote down a series of visions. They came to him through an elderly woman who turned out to be the Church itself, and later through a figure called the Shepherd. Their message: one further chance to repent after baptism, offered now, before that door closes.

dates.display: First Apology c. 153-157; died c. 165 - the best-anchored dating in this world's whole source set

names.name: Justin Martyr (First Apology c. 153-157, Dialogue with Trypho before his death c. 165, per Minns and Parvis)

voices.hedge: Justin's own account of coming to belief - years of searching among the philosophers before a flame was kindled in his soul - is this world's only first-person conversion story. It comes from a man with the education and free time to go looking. No comparable account survives from anyone without what he had.
voices.text: Justin was a philosopher. He kept wearing his philosopher's cloak after he came to believe. He described what a Sunday gathering in Rome actually looked like: reading, a sermon, prayer, the thanksgiving over bread and cup, a collection for those in need. He wrote it all in an open letter to the emperor himself. He died for the name he defended.

dates.died: c. 155-156 (traditional) or 167 (Chronicon) - both carried, neither forced
dates.display: martyred c. 155-156 by the traditional dating; Eusebius's Chronicon gives 167

names.name: Polycarp (Letter to the Philippians; the Martyrdom of Polycarp)

voices.hedge: Even the tradition's own account of his death uses a familiar convention this world's own record does not hide: a fire that arches like a ship's sail, blood that puts out flames. The community's own memory of what his death meant is the real evidence. The staged details are not a transcript.
voices.text: Polycarp led the church at Smyrna. His own letter to the Philippians names him only alongside its other elders, never as bishop - though Ignatius, writing separately, addresses him as one. When his own city turned on him, he refused to curse Christ and was burned. Before his own courage is told, the same letter names a different man who volunteered for trial and lost his nerve when the moment came.

tile.text: From about 70 to 200 CE, Christians in Antioch, the cities of Asia Minor and Rome gathered in households. No central body ruled them. Letters carried by hand held them together. After the apostles died, these churches had not yet settled who should lead. Ignatius's letters urged one bishop with elders beside him, while at Rome, early letters show a council of elders leading. At Corinth, some elders were removed from office. We know this only from Rome's letter, which argued that men who had served blamelessly should not have been removed. Corinth's side does not survive. Communities kept the Lord's table differently, too. One community's manual gives thanks over the cup before the bread, and tells no story of a supper. Being a Christian could at times bring real danger. In one province, a governor had two enslaved women tortured for answers. In another, Ignatius's letters say he was marched under armed guard toward death.
